transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-07
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~78 min
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ellen Cho (Redwood SE), Jordan Nguyen (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (Hydra Head of Platform), Marcus Wu (Hydra SRE), Priya Singh (Hydra ML Infra), Diego Alvarez (Product), Sara Kim (Security)

--- Auto Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Redwood and Hydra ran through specific p95/p99 incidents. Primary hypothesis: intermittent network multi-hop (cross-zone/cross-region) + KV cache cold/shard imbalance creating tails. Discussed mitigation: streaming chunk sizing, prefix KV warming, adaptive batching with hotkey awareness, quantization fallback to FP16 in edge cases, keepalive/socket reuse, and NLB vs ALB behavior. Agreed on lab tests.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we wanted to use this time to walk through the p95/p99 spikes you saw last week and, and the odd jitter around bursts. I have Ellen and Jordan with me. Ellen is going to start with what we saw in our quick replay.
[00:18] Ellen: Cool. So quick context, we replayed the requests from Oct 1–3 window, focusing on long-tail responses. You'll see two modes: steady state traffic where batching keeps latency low, and burst mode where a handful of requests hit cold kv entries or cross a router that adds 30–80 ms.
[00:35] Marcus: That's exactly what we're seeing. Most of our pods are in a single region but the KV service is sharded across two zones for DR, sometimes requests go to the secondary and back which seems to line up with the p99 spikes.
[00:50] Priya: Yeah and to add, the model is a 30B variant sharded across two GPUs, we use 8-bit quantization in prod and sometimes the runtime falls back to cpu for some ops during quantized reprojections. That adds another 50–200 ms occasionally.
[01:10] Jordan: Right and that fallback path is big — if quant ops aren't on the fast kernel path we hit memcpy and CPU scheduling delays. We noticed these after longer sequences where KV cache wasn't capturing prefixes.
[01:28] Lena: Do you think it's more network hop related or the quantization fallback? Our SLO is 90ms p95 and 250ms p99, and some bursts are above that.
[01:40] Ellen: My read is both, in series. A cross-zone hop adds a base delta and then a cache miss can amplify it. Streaming behavior complicates it: when we stream tokens the RTTs show many small writes and flushes which are sensitive to head-of-line blocking on the client LB.
[02:05] Samir: Let's walk through the streaming vs non-streaming case. In streaming we flush small chunks, which lowers perceived latency for the first tokens but can increase tail if the network or LB amplifies packetization overhead. In non-streaming (full response) batching hides some variance but increases first-token latency.
[02:28] Diego: Is there a sweet spot in chunk size that we should try? We observed p99 improves with 64–128 token chunking but not always.
[02:39] Ellen: 64–128 is often a good starting point; but it's also client TCP window, Nagle, and HTTP/2 flow control. For our runtime we suggest testing 64 token chunks, with a 50ms flush threshold. That avoids thousands of tiny writes but keeps streaming responsive.
[03:03] Marcus: Another concern: we have a mesh in front of the inference fleet, sidecars doing mTLS. Could sidecar buffering be adding 10–40 ms per hop sometimes?
[03:16] Jordan: Absolutely. Sidecar queues, repeated TLS handshake renewals if keepalive is low, and socket churn all cause jitter. If you can keep long-lived connections and tweak keepalive, you often remove a lot of noise.
[03:31] Priya: On the KV cache side, our hotkey distribution is skewed. A small percentage of prefixes are responsible for 30% of traffic. When those keys fall off the prefix cache because of TTL or eviction, we see increased latency for that tail.
[03:49] Ellen: That's the classic hotkey problem. Options: increase prefix cache size for hot prefixes, use active warming, or move those hot prefixes onto a local in-memory cache on the serving node. We also support async prefetch so on a prefix miss you can transparently load next likely keys.
[04:11] Lena: Warming seems low-effort. What's the tradeoff CPU/memory wise?
[04:17] Jordan: Prefetch/warm will cost memory and potentially extra read ops, but avoids cold path network hops. For your skew I recommend local in-memory LRU for top 1% prefixes and async prefetch for the next 5–10%.
[04:33] Marcus: For network hops, we traced a p99 spike to a path that went us-west-2 -> partner-network -> us-west-1 then back. There was a NAT and firewall in between. That was an odd multi-hop.
[04:49] Samir: That multi-hop explains delta variance. For private deployments we generally advise minimizing cross-region KV hops and colocating shards where traffic originates, or using read-replicas for local region reads.
[05:06] Diego: We run in VPC with an on-prem DR link — could the VPN overlay be causing packet reordering?
[05:13] Ellen: Yes, overlay networks and reordering can cause head-of-line blocking at the TCP layer which amplifies tail. MTU mismatches and fragmentation exacerbate this. Check your path MTU and avoid PMTU blackholes.
[05:28] Sara: From security perspective we need to ensure any warming/prefetch preserves data residency and doesn't leak keys. How do you handle encryption in-flight?
[05:37] Jordan: All traffic can be mTLS. For KMS we integrate with customer-managed keys; warming prefetch happens inside the VPC so policy controls apply. We'll share the security note and the prefetch design so you can review.
[05:52] Marcus: For benchmarking, we want to reproduce the exact multi-hop. Is Redwood able to inject artificial latency and packet reordering in your lab?
[06:00] Samir: Yes, our bench harness supports network shaping to simulate cross-region hops, packet loss, and variable jitter. We'll provide a topology script.
[06:12] Priya: On quantization side, we saw the runtime sometimes selects a slower kernel for certain attention patterns. Could that be model-architecture dependent?
[06:23] Ellen: Yep. Some attention variants and rotary embeddings cause less efficient kernel paths in quantized mode. The runtime tries to pick best kernel; sometimes we fallback to a safer FP16 kernel which is slower. We should look at op-level profiles to see which ops triggered the fallback.
[06:41] Jordan: Also worth checking is padding and sequence length distribution. If your sequences vary a lot, batching may add padding overhead which can hide compute delays but also mask tail causality.
[06:56] Lena: Does Redwood support adaptive batching that considers prefix cache hits?
[07:03] Ellen: We do. Adaptive batching can split batches when hotkey misses are detected or when latency SLOs are near breach. The idea is to isolate hotkey misses so they don't inflate everyone's latency.
[07:19] Marcus: Could adaptive batching increase cost? If we split more often, GPU utilization drops.
[07:26] Samir: There's always tradeoff. We can tune the policy to only split in rare conditions, or route hotkey traffic to a dedicated pool with different cost profile. That maintains overall efficiency while protecting tails.
[07:43] Diego: For the streaming behavior, is the LB impacting head-of-line blocking? We use an ALB fronting the service.
[07:50] Jordan: ALBs do HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 but some ALBs are less friendly with long half-open connections in streaming scenarios. NLB with TCP passthrough often yields more consistent RTT, but you lose some HTTP features. Worth testing.
[08:08] Priya: Any notes on serialization and tokenization costs? We see occasional CPU spikes on tokenization for long prompts.
[08:16] Ellen: Yes, client-side tokenization or server-side tokenization cost can matter. If you're doing server-side tokenization and it's single-threaded in the container, that spikes request latency. Consider moving tokenization to a side pool or pre-tokenizing on the client when possible.
[08:31] Lena: For on-prem, how different is the guidance? We don't control the full network there.
[08:37] Samir: On-prem requires more careful topology planning: collocate KV and model shards, avoid NAT in the critical path, ensure consistent MTU, and apply warmers. Our private deployment pack has a checklist. We'll share that.
[08:52] Marcus: Let's run through a concrete test matrix. We want to run: baseline (no shaping), cross-region latency 50ms, cross-region 120ms, packet reorder 0.1%, and sidecar enabled/disabled. Also streaming chunk sizes 16/64/128 and batching window 10/50/100ms.
[09:14] Ellen: Great matrix. We'll add quant mode: int8 vs fp16 and with/without fallback. Also prefix cache sizes and hotkey local cache on/off.
[09:27] Jordan: We'll recommend metrics to capture: p50/p95/p99 for first token and last token, CPU steal, GPU kernel time distribution, op-level trace for attention, TCP retransmits, and socket churn.
[09:45] Priya: One more oddity — sometimes a pod shows long GC pauses in the sidecar which then cascades. Could GC be the culprit for a subset of tails?
[09:55] Samir: Definitely. Sidecar GC, python GIL pauses, or misconfigured JVMs can cause tail spikes. Pinning sidecars and tuning GC/heap or moving to non-blocking runtimes helps.
[10:09] Lena: Any quick wins we can implement before the lab?
[10:12] Ellen: Short list: 1) Increase prefix cache for known hot prefixes, 2) enable longer keepalive and connection reuse, 3) test NLB vs ALB in a small canary, 4) pre-warm top prefixes daily. Those are low-risk.
[10:28] Marcus: We'll try the keepalive and pre-warm this week.
[10:31] Diego: Can you also share a small script to simulate hotkey churn? We want to cause eviction quickly to see behavior.
[10:37] Samir: Yes, we'll include a hotkey churn script in the harness.
[10:43] Sara: From security, warming/prefetch must respect token scope and not cross tenancy. We need a design doc.
[10:50] Jordan: We'll write the design note and include the ACL and KMS flow.
[10:55] Ellen: One more nuance on streaming: if you flush too often you increase packets per second and expose you to disruption from early drops. A small smoothing buffer (50–100ms) often reduces p99.
[11:10] Marcus: Noted.
[11:12] Priya: For quantization fallbacks, is there a way to detect before runtime that a particular op will fallback?
[11:18] Jordan: With op-level dry-runs and preflight profiling we can predict kernel availability for the hardware. We'll run a dry profile of your model on our runtime and flag risky ops.
[11:29] Lena: Great. Let's schedule the lab and who should attend?
[11:33] Samir: Recommend a small group: two Redwood SEs (Ellen + Jordan), one Redwood AE (Samir), Hydra: Marcus, Priya, and one infra eng (Lena or Diego). We'll set two hours.
[11:48] Ellen: Ok I'll draft the test plan and share. We'll also include dashboards and alert thresholds so you can watch p99 live.
[11:59] Diego: What about cost implications of dedicating a pool for hotkeys? We need a rough estimate.
[12:05] Samir: We'll provide a delta cost estimate based on GPU hours and expected request mix. That will be in the harness output.
[12:14] Sara: Security doc timeline?
[12:17] Samir: We'll share SOC2 summary and private deploy checklist by 10/09 and the detailed design for prefetch by 10/13.
[12:27] Priya: Anything else?
[12:29] Lena: No, that covers it. Thanks.
[12:31] Samir: Wrap-up: Redwood sends harness + scripts, Hydra shares topology and traces, schedule lab week of Oct 19. Action items in the doc. Thanks all.
